 Pinned Isabel Kershner Johnatan Reiss Aaron Boxerman Qasim Nauman and Leo Sands 
 Here’s the latest. 
 Israel’s political leaders were bracing for weeks of negotiations over a new government, as initial results on Wednesday showed no clear winner in a tightly fought election that many have described as a make-or-break moment for the country.
 By Wednesday evening in Israel, election officials had counted about 90 percent of the ballots. Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s hard-line bloc of parties held a modest lead in seats over the opposition bloc led by Gadi Eisenkot, but it appears that neither coalition will win the 61 seats needed to secure a straightforward majority in the Knesset, Israel’s Parliament. 
 That means both leaders would need to find support from outside their coalitions to form a government. Two Arab parties were on track to win as many as 19 seats, a strong showing that potentially gives them an important role in the negotiations, even though most Jewish parties were not eager to enter an alliance with them. 
 Some of Mr. Netanyahu’s allies have floated the idea that he could join Mr. Eisenkot and other centrists to form a broad unity government to stay in power. For Mr. Netanyahu, who will remain a caretaker prime minister until a government is formed, that would be a comfortable scenario.
 Mr. Eisenkot faces a dilemma. He has denounced Mr. Netanyahu as unfit to lead Israel, but he has also objected to partnering with Arab parties in a potential coalition. On Wednesday, Mr. Eisenkot did not explicitly mention the Arab parties but said he was focused on forming a government that was both Zionist and committed to universal military conscription, a message that rules out alliances with both Arab and ultra-Orthodox Jewish parties.
 The Joint List, an alliance of Arab parties that has emerged as a potential kingmaker according to preliminary results, said it would “do everything in its power” to remove Mr. Netanyahu from office. That could signal a willingness to back Mr. Eisenkot’s bid to form an anti-Netanyahu coalition, even if its lawmakers have not been invited to join it. 
 The final tally of votes is not expected to be finished before Thursday evening. Lengthy negotiations are likely to follow as political parties try to assemble a governing majority. If those talks fail, the country could head to a second round of elections — a scenario that has played out before. 
 Here’s what else we are covering:
 Vote count: The nearly 90 percent of votes counted indicate that Mr. Netanyahu’s coalition will receive about 54 seats, Mr. Eisenkot’s bloc will get roughly 49, and the Arab parties could reach as many as 19. But the numbers could still shift.
 Parliamentary control: Even if no government is formed, the Israeli Parliament will open on Nov. 10, and Mr. Netanyahu’s opponents could be well-placed to take control of the legislative process. Read more › 
 Herzog’s role: President Isaac Herzog of Israel holds a largely ceremonial position, except after national elections, when it falls to him to select who gets the first crack at forming a new government. Read more › 
 What Israelis think: The day after Israel’s election, almost everyone in the country was asking the same question: What now? The Times spoke to people from across the political spectrum to get a sense of their hopes and fears. Read more ›

 Reporting from Jerusalem Arab parties’ surprisingly strong showing means Israel’s Arab minority cannot be ignored. 
 Image Voting in the predominantly Arab town of Tayibe during the Israeli election on Tuesday. Credit... Ahmad Gharabli/Agence France-Presse — Getty Images For decades, Israel’s Arab parties have been relegated to the margins of Israeli political life, often sitting on the sidelines while Jewish parties assembled a governing coalition in Parliament and picked a prime minister.
 Heading into Israel’s pivotal election on Tuesday, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu warned his supporters that the Arabs were “trying to steal the election,” though electoral officials said there were no reports of widespread irregularities. He repeatedly invoked the specter of Arab voters to galvanize his right-wing base, vowing to keep them out of power.
 Mr. Netanyahu’s leading rival, Gadi Eisenkot, largely declined to answer whether he would partner with Arab parties if necessary to topple the Netanyahu government, though he said none met his conditions as potential allies.
 But record turnout on Tuesday by supporters of the Arab parties looks to deliver them their largest vote totals in generations, possibly since Israel’s establishment 78 years ago.
 Now, the Arab minority represents a political reality that cannot be ignored.
 Turnout in the Arab community, which represents about 20 percent of Israeli citizens, appears to have translated into a stunning windfall of parliamentary seats — potentially as many as 19 combined between the two leading parties, Raam and the Joint List alliance. The Arab parties have 10 seats in the outgoing Parliament.
 Israel’s future could turn in part on whether Mr. Eisenkot decides to take the political risks of partnering with them. Without their support, Mr. Eisenkot and his alliance will almost certainly fall short of the 61-seat majority required in the 120-seat Parliament to form a new government and end Mr. Netanyahu’s hold on power. Mr. Netanyahu’s alliance also looks to fall short of 61 seats.
 Many Israeli Jews have long objected to building a governing coalition that relies on Arab party backing for a majority. Some say a Jewish state should be ruled exclusively by Jews. Some cite national security reasons, questioning whether Arab leaders who see themselves as part of the wider Palestinian people can be entrusted with crucial matters of state.
 Those objections became even more acute after the Hamas-led Oct. 7, 2023, attacks on Israel and the subsequent rightward shift in Israeli politics. Both Raam and some members of the Joint List condemned the assault, although they have also been highly critical of how Israel has conducted its war against Hamas in Gaza.
 The Arab parties for many years were themselves reluctant to join governments that oversaw the Israeli occupation of the West Bank and Gaza. And turnout among Arab Israelis has traditionally been lower than Jewish turnout, reflecting doubts about their ability to influence national decision-making.
 Raam, a socially conservative party with roots in Islamist politics, has achieved some acceptance in Israel’s mainstream by putting less emphasis on the cause of Palestinian statehood. But the Joint List, an alliance of three smaller parties that includes a joint Jewish-Arab leftist faction and a Palestinian nationalist faction, is seen as more antagonistic toward Zionism.
 Initial election results show that the Joint List will be the significantly larger of the two in Parliament.
 “Netanyahu knows that without the Arab parties, there’s no majority to unseat him. That’s why he incites against us,” said Yousef Jabareen, the leader of the Joint List alliance in an interview. “The opposition should reject that incitement.”
 He added: “The ball is now in Eisenkot’s court. Whoever wants to remove Netanyahu and change his policies — we are ready to cooperate to topple his government.”
 Political analysts say the Joint List would be more likely to support Eisenkot from outside the governing coalition, for instance by agreeing to block any no-confidence votes. There is some precedent for this: In the 1990s, then Prime Minister Yitzhak Rabin relied on Arab lawmakers to prevent the collapse of his own minority government.
 Arab citizens, some of whom view themselves as both Israeli and Palestinian, experience a tension that can cut to the heart of daily life. Unlike Palestinians in the West Bank — who live under Israeli military rule — Arab Israelis can vote, and some have held high office, including on the country’s Supreme Court.
 But they largely live in separate cities and towns from Jewish Israelis and retain tight familial and historical bonds with Palestinians in the West Bank and Gaza. Many view themselves as second-class citizens in the Jewish state, saying they face discrimination in housing as well as neglect in receiving public services.
 Before this year, the largest electoral success recorded by Arab parties was in 2020, when they secured 15 seats. And the first — and so far, only — time an independent Arab party joined the Israeli governing coalition was in 2021, when Mansour Abbas, the leader of Raam , joined Mr. Netanyahu’s rivals to unseat him in favor of a short-lived government.
 Mr. Abbas has since worked to make his party more acceptable to Israeli Jews. He has recognized Israel’s Jewish character as a fact of life and publicly considered integrating Arabs into the country’s mandatory national service, in particular community service.
 In a bold move during the election campaign, he named Jewish lawmaker Yoav Segalovitz — a former senior police officer and centrist Zionist — as the number two on the Raam candidate list.
 But if exit polls and initial results are correct, Raam’s support would not be enough to give Mr. Eisenkot’s bloc a parliamentary majority. He would also have to rely on the Joint List to topple Mr. Netanyahu. While political analysts say that Mr. Eisenkot might be willing to bring Raam onboard, he would struggle to keep his bloc with him if he made common cause with the Joint List, even if he wanted to, because this could provoke too much political blowback from many Jewish voters.
 “There’s a shift in Arab politics, an attempt to get closer to the Jewish Zionist mainstream. It’s just that the other side is not willing to do so,” said Thair Abu Rass, an expert on Israel’s Arab politics. “There’s no partner on the Jewish side to create an alternative reality.”

 Gadi Eisenkot, the main challenger to Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, said on Wednesday that he was focused on forming a government that would be both Zionist and committed to universal military conscription, a message that rules out alliances with Arab and ultra-Orthodox Jewish parties.
 The Joint List, an alliance of Arab parties that has emerged as a potential kingmaker according to preliminary results, said it would “do everything in its power” to remove Netanyahu from office. That could signal a willingness to back Eisenkot’s bid to form an anti-Netanyahu coalition, even though it remained unclear if the Joint List lawmakers would be invited in.

 Reporting from Tel Aviv The vote count has progressed, but is not expected to conclude before Thursday evening in Israel. The counting process has two tiers: Election authorities have counted more than 88 percent of ballots cast at polling stations across Israel. That count is expected to be completed in the coming hours, possibly before Thursday morning in Israel, according to a representative of the Central Election Committee.
 But a separate set of ballots — those cast at special voting sites, including military bases, prisons, and hospitals — has yet to be counted. Authorities estimate that these number over 400,000, or roughly 7 percent of all ballots cast. Their counting is not expected to be completed before Thursday evening, when the final official results may be released.

 Reporting from Jerusalem
 Israel’s opposition may not be able to form a government, but it still could control Parliament. 
 Image Empty seats at the Knesset, the Israeli Parliament, following a vote to dissolve the assembly in May ahead of the elections. Credit... Ronen Zvulun/Reuters The initial results in the Israeli election released on Wednesday showed that there was no outright winner, and it may take weeks for it to become clear who will be able to form the next government.
 But even if no government is formed, the Israeli Parliament will open on Nov. 10, and Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s opponents could be well-placed to take control of the legislative process.
 The Parliament, or Knesset, will open with a swearing in of the 120 lawmakers. Both of the main blocs of Jewish parties likely fell short of winning a majority of seats, and both are reluctant to form a government that relies on a partnership with two predominantly Arab parties.
 But even if the main anti-Netanyahu bloc, led by Gadi Eisenkot , does not join with Arab parties to form a government, they remain united on some issues. If they join forces in parliamentary votes, they could stymie some of the Netanyahu government’s most contentious policies.
 The first requirement would be to choose a new speaker of the house, so that the opposition could take control of the parliamentary agenda, key committees and start enacting laws, experts say.
 “I’m not saying it’s a good scenario to take the Knesset and not be able to form the government,” said Gayil Talshir, a political scientist at the Hebrew University of Jerusalem who is advising the opposition. “It’s a disaster. But this is the hand they are dealt, and they have to play it.”
 One of the issues on which Mr. Eisenkot’s bloc and Arab parties agree — beyond wanting to unseat Mr. Netanyahu — is the need for an independent state inquiry into the government’s failure to prevent the Hamas-led attack on Israel on Oct. 7, 2023.
 Mr. Netanyahu, who has never taken responsibility for his government’s lapses in failing to stop the attack, has refused to allow such an inquiry. In the new Parliament, the opposition parties could work to establish one.
 Another point that both sides agree on is a desire to overturn laws to carry out a sweeping overhaul of the judiciary .
 Supporters of the Netanyahu government’s divisive plan said it was necessary to rein in what they saw as an overactive judiciary, to restore the balance between the branches of government and give more power to elected officials. Critics, however, said the proposed measures would remove checks on government power.
 “Damaging legislation and damaging practices were introduced, but they can still be reversed,” said Yohanan Plesner, president of the Israel Democracy Institute, a nonpartisan research group.
 Other contentious laws that could be challenged include one that politicized the process for appointing Supreme Court judges, and others that weakened the authority of the attorney general and expanded the authority of rabbinical courts.
 Opposition members have also raised the idea of introducing legislation to bar a candidate charged with a crime from forming a government or to limit a prime minister to two terms in office.
 Both of those efforts would be aimed at Mr. Netanyahu, Israel’s longest serving prime minister who is standing trial on corruption charges.
 But such proposals would be problematic, experts say, because they could be seen as laws targeting Mr. Netanyahu personally and so would likely be challenged in Israel’s Supreme Court.
 Such laws would also not apply retroactively, say, to a candidate who had been indicted in the past, Suzie Navot, an Israeli professor of constitutional law, said.
 “They would not pass easily,” she said. She added the court could postpone such laws so that they could only come into effect in the next Knesset, or even strike them down.
 David M. Halbfinger contributed reporting.

 Natan Odenheimer reported from Jaffa, Gabby Sobelman from Rehovot and Heedo Abu Laban from Jerusalem
 Israelis ponder an uncertain future as no clear winner emerges in the voting. 
 Image A day after polling, Israelis were uncertain about the future, as no party appeared headed for a majority in Parliament. A campaign ad features Gadi Eisenkot. Credit... David Goldman/Associated Press The day after Israel’s election, many supporters of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu felt relief that the results tallied so far showed that the opposition’s path to forming a new government was narrow. Others who had hoped for a decisive opposition victory were crushed by results that could well lead to a political stalemate.
 Almost everyone was asking the same question: What now?
 “I’m hopeful,” said Merav Katz, 57, a Netanyahu supporter, as she got her hair straightened at a salon in Jaffa. She said she would like to see an all-Jewish unity government with some opposition parties but not including the Arab parties, which made a strong showing.
 Ms. Katz expressed a sentiment shared by many right-wing voters: An indecisive result among Israeli Jewish voters would put pressure on the opposition to join a coalition with Mr. Netanyahu to avoid another round of elections.
 The preliminary results show that Mr. Netanyahu’s hard-right alliance and the bloc of parties led by Gadi Eisenkot, his main opponent, are both likely to be short of the 61 seats needed to form a majority government.
 Mr. Eisenkot could extend his hand to the two main Arab parties to form a minority government. Arab citizens, fearing another far-right government, turned out in historically high numbers.
 Still, it would be difficult for Mr. Eisenkot, who ran on a center-right campaign, to form an alliance with the largest Arab party, the Joint List, whose leaders often harshly criticize Israel’s actions in Gaza and the West Bank.
 At the salon in Jaffa, Ms. Katz’s hairdresser, Saado Zorob, 48, an Arab citizen, said that Jewish Israelis seemed happy to be treated by Arab physicians at hospitals and to eat at Arab restaurants but that many were unwilling to give Arab citizens a role in charting the country’s future.
 “I feel like garbage,” he said as he was blow drying Ms. Katz’s hair. He added that he wished Mr. Eisenkot had the courage to form a government with the Arab caucus. Another election might benefit Mr. Netanyahu. “I’m worried that if the deadlock yields another round of elections, many Arabs will stay home,” he said
 Image A Likud party campaign ad featuring Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and President Trump. Credit... Ohad Zwigenberg/Associated Press To many supporters of Mr. Netanyahu, a Jewish-Arab coalition would be a nightmare.
 Yakov Matzlawi, 51, a Likud member who manages a men’s undergarment stall in a market in Ramla, near Tel Aviv, said the mood among Netanyahu supporters he knew was subdued. Mr. Netanyahu didn’t lose, he said, but he didn’t win either, and many of on the right were still confused about what the results meant for the country.
 “What’s important is that we remain in the game,” he said.
 Five miles south, in the city of Rehovot, Shira Barkan, 49, a therapist who wanted to see Mr. Netanyahu’s government fall, sat with her teenage daughter at an açai shop, their bowls only half eaten. “I don’t have much of an appetite,” she said.
 She had gone to bed the night before hopeful, she said, but “woke up in the morning with Bibi again,” using Mr. Netanyahu’s nickname. In her view, Mr. Netanyahu’s extremist government was leading Israel toward global isolation.
 “Israelis are amazing people, and they deserve leadership that will not only protect us from external wrongs, but also stop its own wrongdoing,” she said.

 Reporting from Jerusalem Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s Likud party is persisting with unproven allegations that Israel’s Arab voters have “stolen the elections.” Israel’s official elections committee has said there was no indication of widespread irregularities in the election on Tuesday. On Wednesday, the Likud again said that Arab parties — which are expected to receive a historically high number of parliamentary seats — had stolen the vote and called for the police and intelligence services to investigate.
 Analysts say that Netanyahu is trying to de-legitimize votes by Arab citizens of Israel, fearing that his leading Jewish Israeli opponents might try to link up with the newly empowered Arab political bloc in an effort to unseat him.
 Oct. 28, 2026, 12:21 p.m. ET Aaron Boxerman 
 Reporting from Jerusalem Netanyahu didn’t win the Israeli election. But he’s far from out. 
 Image Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu of Israel speaking to supporters in Jerusalem on election night. Credit... Chris Mcgrath/Getty Images Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu of Israel fell short of outright victory on Tuesday night. But he has still emerged with a good chance of clinging to power.
 Mr. Netanyahu, 77, has plenty of political blessings to count after the vote. His Likud party is set to remain the largest in the Israeli Parliament, defying the pre-election polls. His rivals, led by the former general Gadi Eisenkot, secured far less support and have been left more divided than expected.
 Analysts say the result, with neither bloc securing enough votes to form a clear majority, could easily lead to weeks or months of political gridlock — a scenario that suits Mr. Netanyahu just fine. He will remain in charge as caretaker prime minister until a new government is formed or new elections have to be held.
 It is a remarkable turnaround for Mr. Netanyahu, whose critics blamed him for failing to prevent the Hamas-led attack on Oct. 7, 2023, the deadliest day in Israeli history. A consummate political survivor of more than three decades in Israeli politics, Mr. Netanyahu is famous for out-negotiating and manipulating almost every opponent who has tried to end his rule.
 “Netanyahu is still in the driver’s seat,” said Natan Sachs, an expert on Israeli politics at the Middle East Institute, a Washington-based research group. “He’s still in control of most events, and that’s where he likes to be.”
 Mr. Netanyahu, the longest serving prime minister in Israeli history, still has some headaches. The hard-line coalition he formed in 2022 — the most far-right in Israeli history — is set to lose its majority in Israel’s 120-member Parliament.
 Mr. Netanyahu could also end up losing if Mr. Eisenkot, whose bloc trails the prime minister’s coalition by several seats, chooses to work with the Arab parties that performed better than ever to oust him.
 But Mr. Eisenkot is likely to struggle to form such an alliance, given how Israeli public opinion has shifted since the Oct. 7 attacks. Even though Arab leaders in Israel generally condemned the attacks, many Jewish Israelis still regard partnering with them as unacceptable.
 “Netanyahu knew he was going to have a weaker bloc. But he knew that his goal, even if he couldn’t get a 61-seat majority, would be to prevent his rivals from forming a government,” said Mazal Mualem, who has written a biography of Mr. Netanyahu. “And it seems he’s succeeded.”
 All this was hard to imagine just three years ago. Mr. Netanyahu’s public standing plunged after the Oct. 7 attacks, when 1,200 in Israel were killed and 250 were taken hostage, igniting the war in Gaza. Even fervent supporters of the prime minister feared his time in office would end because of his failure to prevent the catastrophe.
 Mr. Netanyahu, however, has tenaciously clambered his way back without accepting any responsibility for the devastating security lapse. Instead, he blamed the assault on Israeli security chiefs, launched a series of military campaigns in Lebanon and Iran that killed some of Israel’s most significant foes, and ran his electoral campaign focused on amplifying fears of Israel’s Arab parties.
 On Tuesday, a swath of Jewish Israelis threw their support behind him, defying Mr. Netanyahu’s critics at home and abroad. The prime minister gave a fiery speech overnight on Wednesday as initial exit polls showed he had outperformed expectations vowing to establish “a patriotic, strong, right-wing government.”
 While a slight shift in the results could upend the electoral map, Mr. Netanyahu has several options for how he might stay in power.
 One path would be to try to block any new government from being formed, forcing Israel to hold new elections. Mr. Netanyahu’s opponents — who threw years of energy and planning into the recent vote only to fall short — would struggle to do better in a new vote, analysts say.
 “There’s a general sense that this was the opposition’s big chance,” Mr. Sachs said. “From Netanyahu’s perspective, he can throw the dice again and again.”
 Another option would be to form a unity government with one of his opponents. But that will be difficult as long as Mr. Netanyahu insists on staying in the prime minister’s office.
 Mr. Eisenkot has vowed not to serve under Mr. Netanyahu, although a national emergency — such as renewed fighting with Iran — could change that calculation.
 Mr. Netanyahu could also try to pick off potential right-wing defectors from Mr. Eisenkot’s bloc. These include opposition leaders who served in previous Netanyahu governments, such as Naftali Bennett, who leads the center-right Together party, and Avigdor Liberman, who leads the right-wing Yisrael Beitenu.
 Both men are right-wing supporters of Jewish settlements in the Israeli-occupied West Bank. Both refrained from explicitly endorsing Mr. Eisenkot, Mr. Netanyahu’s main challenger, as the opposition bloc’s candidate for prime minister.
 But rekindling their old partnerships with Mr. Netanyahu would be difficult. Both Mr. Bennett and Mr. Liberman have considerable bad blood with the prime minister. They have also been strident in demanding an independent commission of inquiry into the failures surrounding the Oct. 7 disaster, which Mr. Netanyahu has resisted.
 Isabel Kershner contributed reporting.

 SKIP ADVERTISEMENT Oct. 28, 2026, 11:20 a.m. ET Adam Rasgon 
 Reporting from Tel Aviv
 Gadi Eisenkot, Netanyahu’s main rival, has no easy options. 
 Image Gadi Eisenkot addresses voters on Wednesday after exit polls from Israel’s election were released. Credit... Amir Levy/Getty Images Gadi Eisenkot, the leading figure in Israel’s political opposition, had hoped voters would deliver him a clear mandate to form a government, and begin a new era without Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu at the helm.
 The initial results show, however, that Mr. Eisenkot and his allies have no easy path to power. They face a dilemma: To secure enough seats in parliament to form a government, they either need to cooperate with Arab-led parties — anathema to many Israelis — or join with Mr. Netanyahu or members of his right-wing alliance.
 “He’s in a Catch-22,” said Shira Efron, chair of Israel policy at the RAND Corporation. “He doesn’t have a lot of great options.”
 If Mr. Eisenkot and the opposition were to join forces with the Arab parties, the results so far suggest that they would need the support of both the major ones: the socially conservative Raam party and the Joint List, a coalition of three factions. 
 “After Oct. 7, Israeli society will not accept that,” said Shalom Yerushalmi, a veteran political writer at the news site Zman Yisrael, referring to the 2023 Hamas-led attack on southern Israel. “There’s no chance.”
 Many Israelis are opposed to any government that would rely on parties that are not Zionist, and would not want those parties to influence security policies or foreign affairs. On the campaign trail, a number of opposition members pledged never to agree to such an arrangement.
 Although Raam’s leader, Mansour Abbas , has taken positions more amenable to Zionist members of the opposition, including putting less emphasis on the Palestinian cause, the Joint List has refused to make similar compromises. 
 In the aftermath of Oct. 7, the leaders of the parties in the Joint List reacted in different ways. Ayman Odeh, who was the head of Hadash, referred to “ Hamas’s murderous attack ” in an opinion essay for The New York Times. Ahmad Tibi, the leader of Taal, said Arab citizens were against targeting civilians. 
 Sami Abou Shahadeh, the chairman of Balad, said the attack was “an important, historic event in the military sense,” though he later condemned the attack after the Israeli Supreme Court discussed disqualifying him from running for parliament. 
 The prospect of Mr. Eisenkot setting up a unity government with Mr. Netanyahu or members of his bloc appears to be just as challenging. He made Mr. Netanyahu’s record a central theme of his campaign, saying the Israeli prime minister should “go home” and suggesting that he was unfit to lead the country.
 Mr. Eisenkot may be able to come to an agreement with Mr. Netanyahu that excludes some of the most extreme elements of the current Israeli coalition from government — such as the far-right cabinet members Itamar Ben-Gvir and Bezalel Smotrich. But to do so would be to go back on a theme of his campaign.
 “If he goes for a unity government, he would be destroying the whole narrative he has built,” Mr. Yerushalmi said.
 Mr. Eisenkot could attempt to convince members of Mr. Netanyahu’s party, Likud, to defect to his side, but that seems unlikely because the long-serving Israeli leader has in the past been highly effective at holding his coalition together. 
 Mr. Netanyahu’s coalition also includes some ultra-Orthodox parties, which Mr. Eisenkot could try to bring into his bloc. Yet many opposition members are at odds with lawmakers from those parties over the exemptions from military service that many ultra-Orthodox Israelis enjoy.
 Another option for Mr. Eisenkot and his partners is to hold out for a new round of elections in the hope of achieving a more favorable result. But that scenario, analysts said, was fraught with pitfalls — Mr. Eisenkot’s supporters, including those living abroad, may be feel less motivated to show up to vote again.

 Reporting from Jerusalem
 news analysis
 Here are 4 takeaways from the election. 
 Gadi Eisenkot, a former Israeli military chief of staff, and Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. Amir Cohen/Reuters; Alexi J. Rosenfeld/Getty Images The results of Israel’s pivotal parliamentary election will not be finalized at least until Thursday and it could be weeks until it is clear what kind of government will be formed and who will lead it. But some conclusions are already inescapable.
 Arab citizens of Israel turned out to vote in record numbers. Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s Likud party gobbled up many votes that his right-wing and Orthodox Jewish coalition partners had expected would be theirs. And the pre-election polls failed to anticipate both phenomena.
 Much could still change. But with most of the votes counted by Wednesday afternoon, here are some initial takeaways.
 Netanyahu didn’t win, but Eisenkot lost.
 Mr. Netanyahu’s coalition appears to have shrunk considerably from the 64 parliamentary seats that it won in 2022: The latest results show it with around 54, well short of a majority in the 120-member Knesset, or Parliament. But he could wind up in better position to form a government than his chief rival, Gadi Eisenkot .
 Mr. Eisenkot, a former Israeli military chief of staff, had two goals in the election: to lead the Jewish opposition parties to an outright majority or at least get very close to one, and to make sure his own party, Yashar, got more votes than any other. He failed on both counts, the initial results indicate.
 Reuven Hazan, a political science professor at the Hebrew University of Jerusalem, said that it had been hard to imagine better conditions for Mr. Eisenkot’s alliance ahead of the election. Mr. Netanyahu and his coalition were weighed down by anger over the Hamas-led Oct. 7, 2023 attacks and their failure to do more to free Israeli hostages; by anger over ultra-Orthodox Jewish draft-dodging in wartime; and by outrage over the government’s efforts to neuter the judiciary and allow growing settler violence against Palestinians in the Israeli-occupied West Bank, he said.
 “The anti-Netanyahu camp had an election handed to them on a silver platter, and they still lost,” Mr. Hazan said. “Israelis have sent an ambiguous message: ‘We don’t really like the current government, but we don’t see a viable alternative.’”
 Netanyahu’s coalition shrank, but he has options.
 As votes were being counted on Wednesday afternoon, Likud was poised to be the largest party in the larger of the two blocs of Jewish-led parties, meaning Mr. Netanyahu could well be given the chance to form a government, Mr. Hazan said.
 The long-serving Israeli premier may try to peel away some of Mr. Eisenkot’s putative partners in order to achieve a majority of 61 seats in Parliament. A number of them are as right-wing as he is, though all have more or less ruled out entering a Netanyahu-led government.
 He could also try to form a national unity government with Mr. Eisenkot — perhaps with the assistance of President Trump, who has praised Mr. Netanyahu as a “warrior prime minister” and has made clear he wants Israel to join the United States in another round of war against Iran.
 Perhaps the most mind-bending option available to Mr. Netanyahu, given that he ran a scaremongering campaign that demonized Arab lawmakers and stoked fears of Arab voter turnout, would be to recruit an Arab party to join him in a government. He nearly did so once before, in 2022.
 “It could very well be that they become indispensable,” said Dahlia Scheindlin, a pollster and political analyst, said of Arab lawmakers. “And Netanyahu has certainly demonstrated his willingness to do anything to stay in power.”

Ohad Zwigenberg/Associated Press Isaac Herzog, Israel’s president, has a largely ceremonial role — except after national elections, when it is his responsibility to choose a potential prime minister and then tasks that person with trying to form a government.
 Since Israelis vote for a party or parties rather than an individual, the person who might lead the country is selected after the ballots are counted and parliamentary seats are allocated to parties according to their proportion of the vote. The president — who is separately elected by the Knesset, Israel’s single-chamber legislature — then convenes party leaders to hear their recommendations for prime minister before choosing someone to form a government.
 While the president can choose the leader of the party that won the most votes, he can also select another leader who seems more likely to assemble a coalition that can secure a vote of confidence in the Knesset . 
 In 2009, President Shimon Peres chose Benjamin Netanyahu — the current prime minister — even though his right-wing Likud party had won fewer votes than the centrist Kadima party.
 Early exit polls on Wednesday suggest a tight race between the far-right coalition led by Mr. Netanyahu and the center-right opposition bloc that has called for change. The opposition bloc includes the Yashar party, led by Gadi Eisenkot. But Mr. Netanyahu’s Likud party appears to have received the most votes, which means he will argue that he should be selected as prime minister.
 Mr. Herzog, whose job is to stay above the political fray, is expected to face a difficult decision. He must discern whether the votes show that the majority of Israelis demanded change or if they indicated a preference for another Netanyahu government.
 Mr. Netanyahu’s governing coalition, the most right-wing in Israel’s history, has drawn international condemnation, heightened tensions with allies and divided Israelis. Mr. Herzog has repeatedly criticized what he has called “ a terrible process of brutalization ” creeping into Israeli society, citing violence by Jewish settlers in the occupied West Bank against Palestinians and the abuse of detainees in Israeli custody, which some far-right ministers in Mr. Netanyahu’s coalition are accused of encouraging.
 The Israeli president, who can grant criminal pardons and commute sentences, has also faced pressure from President Trump , who has called on him to pardon Mr. Netanyahu as he stands trial on corruption charges. Mr. Herzog has respectfully resisted, saying that “Israel is a sovereign state governed by the rule of law.”
 Mr. Netanyahu has long resisted calls for an independent commission of inquiry into the Oct. 7, 2023, Hamas-led attack on Israel that set off a devastating war in Gaza. He has also refused to take responsibility for any failures that led to the attack, angering many Israelis.
